extracted.intended_audience: EPO examiners, patent attorneys, and applicants preparing European patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on meeting the sufficiency of disclosure requirement (Art. 83 EPC / Rule 42) for European patent applications, including how much description, examples, and functional detail are needed so a skilled person can carry out the invention. Covers case‑law principles, burden of proof, and consequences of partial disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed description of at least one way of carrying out the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A detailed description of at least one way of carrying out the invention must be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description should disclose any feature essential for carrying out the invention in sufficient detail to render it apparent to the person skilled in the art how to put the invention into practice. Well‑known ancillary features need not be described. (References: Art. 83; Rule 42(1)(e))

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressed to the person skilled in the art; exclusion of well‑known ancillary details
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the application is addressed to the person skilled in the art, it is neither necessary nor desirable that details of well-known ancillary features are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not clutter the disclosure with routine or conventional details the skilled person would know, but ensure all features essential for carrying out the invention are disclosed with sufficient detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of exemplification required where claims cover a broad field
rubrics_metrics.description: A single example may suffice, but where the claims cover a broad field, the application is not usually regarded as satisfying Art. 83 unless the description gives a number of examples or describes alternative embodiments or variations extending over the area protected by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess on facts and evidence of each case; some very broad fields may be sufficiently exemplified by limited examples, but usually multiple examples or alternatives are needed to support broad claim scopes. (See also F‑IV, 6.3; Art. 83; Rule 42(1)(e))

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to enable performance over the whole area claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must contain, in addition to the examples, sufficient information to allow the person skilled in the art, using common general knowledge, to perform the invention over the whole area claimed without undue burden and without needing inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is required particularly when only limited examples are provided; applicant must enable substantially any embodiment falling within the ambit of the claim. (Case: T 727/95)

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'whole area claimed' and permissible trial-and-error
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'whole area claimed' is to be understood as substantially any embodiment falling within the ambit of a claim, even though a limited amount of trial and error may be permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited trial and error may be acceptable in unexplored fields or where many technical difficulties exist, but the required experimentation must not amount to an undue burden. (Cases: T 226/85; T 409/91)

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic limitations from a sensible reading of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing sufficiency the intrinsic limitations that a sensible reading imposes on the subject‑matter of the independent claims must be taken into consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The skilled person will exclude any embodiment that is meaningless and not consistent with the teaching of the application; sensible claim reading can therefore narrow the practical scope for sufficiency analysis. (Case: T 521/12)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for raising an insufficiency objection (serious doubts & verifiable facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection of lack of sufficient disclosure presupposes that there are serious doubts, substantiated by verifiable facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining divisions must be able to make out a reasoned case based on facts; if they do so, the onus shifts to the applicant to establish that the invention may be performed and repeated over substantially the whole of the claimed range. (Cases: T 409/91; T 694/92; F‑III, 4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and consequences when only part of claimed subject‑matter is disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application is sufficiently disclosed only in respect of a part of the claimed subject‑matter, this may lead to a partial European search report under Rule 63.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases, and in the absence of appropriate amendment, an objection under Rule 63(3) can arise; applicants should amend or otherwise address partial sufficiency to avoid partial search/Rule 63 implications. (Rule 63; B‑VIII, 3.1 and 3.2; H‑II, 5; H‑II, 6.1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of function vs. structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For the requirements of Art. 83 and Rule 42, it is necessary that the invention is described not only in terms of its structure but also in terms of its function, unless the functions of the various parts are immediately apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some technical fields (e.g., computers), a clear description of function may be more appropriate than an over‑detailed description of structure. Where functions are critical to enablement, emphasize functional disclosure so the skilled person can implement the invention.
